object.description: The title page of the book that gave physics its laws. Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy', sets out Newton's three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, and uses them to derive Kepler's planetary orbits, the tides, the shape of the Earth, the precession of the equinoxes and the paths of comets, all from one inverse-square force. The page records how it came to be printed: 'Imprimatur, S. Pepys, Reg. Soc. Præses, Julii 5. 1686', the licence of the Royal Society under its president Samuel Pepys, and 'Jussu Societatis Regiæ ac Typis Josephi Streater', printed by Joseph Streater at the Society's order. In fact the Society had spent its money on a history of fishes, and the astronomer Edmond Halley, who had prodded Newton into writing the book, paid for the printing himself. Newton is named as Lucasian Professor at Trinity College, Cambridge. Only a few hundred copies were printed, in Latin, and they sold for about nine shillings.
facts: Newton wrote the three books in about eighteen months, between 1685 and 1686.
Halley's prompt was a question in 1684: what orbit does an inverse-square force give? Newton answered 'an ellipse', and had already proved it.
Second and third editions followed in 1713 and 1726; Newton's own annotated first edition survives at Trinity College.
The first English translation, by Andrew Motte, appeared in 1729, two years after Newton's death.

tour: Newton's Principia, 1687: three laws of motion and one of gravity, for everything that moves, in one book.
